As of 455 AM Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... An axis of showers storms will progress slowly 
ssewd across cntl NC through early Friday, with an associated risk 
of excessive rain. 

A shortwave trough, evident in GOES-E water vapor satellite data 
over the srn border of ON/QC, will lift newd through the St. 
Lawrence River vicinity through this evening. Rising heights will 
follow the wave and result throughout the lwr Great Lakes, Middle 
Atlantic, and Northeast, with related deamplification and weakening 
of a longwave ern CONUS trough. Cntl NC will be mostly displaced 
from the influence of the shortwave trough but in continued very 
moist and broadly cyclonic flow, with the former highlighted by a 
top 10 all-time observed PW of 2.32" at GSO last evening. Weakly 
veering, uniformly-strong flow of 30-40 kts in the 850-500 mb layer 
will continue to be directed into a similarly-aligned low-level 
frontal zone over the srn Middle Atlantic.  

That low-level frontal zone will tend to consolidate and strengthen, 
as a synoptic cold front now progressing steadily through s-cntl VA 
nears and probably eventually overtakes later today a nearly 
stationary outflow boundary/effective front draped from EDE-FBG-CLT 
in e-cntl through s-cntl NC. The merged front will then settle into, 
and become quasi-stationary over, the ern Carolinas late tonight-
Fri.  

Isentropic lift induced by a 30-35 kt swly low-level jet and WAA 
intersecting the fronts, and a low-level frontogenetical 
circulation, will favor lift in the aforementioned deeply moist 
environment over cntl NC. When combined with only weak nnwly upwind 
propagation vectors resulting from the wind profile noted above, and 
associated slow ssewd propagation of the axis of ongoing convection, 
and a continued conditionally unstable thermodynamic profiles with 
generally 1000-1500 J/kg of MUCAPE, the environment will remain 
conducive for slow-moving convection with risk of flash flooding. 
This risk will be greatest over the Triangle this morning, prior to 
the arrival of the synoptic front from the north and following drier 
air in the low-levels (eg. surface dewpoints now falling through the 
50s-60s throughout nrn and cntl VA). After as much as 4-5" inches of 
rain fell over the nw Piedmont overnight, but with rates 
insufficient to produce any notable flash flooding, the axis of 
convection and risk of flooding appears to have now shifted just 
south of the Triad.  

While most of cntl NC is not outlooked beyond general thunder in the 
latest SWODY1, VWP-observed and SPC/objective mesoanalysis-
corroborated 0-1 km bulk shear of 20-25 kts and 0-1 km SRH of 100-
150 m2/s2 remain favorable for a weak spinup in cells that develop 
and track along the effective front - much like the earlier Johnston 
Co. cell that exhibited a Vrot of 20-25 kts around 2-4 ft ARL and 
necessitated a SVR with TOR possible tag.

It will otherwise remain unseasonably mild and with a chance to set 
record low maximum temperatures over the Piedmont, contrasted by 80s 
in the warm sector from the srn Piedmont to the Sandhills and cntl 
Coastal Plain. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... The slow moving cold front across the Carolinas 
will move across eastern NC and into northern SC resulting in a 
continued threat of rain, focused across southern areas where the 
rain could be locally heavy.

Friday's forecast and possible impacts remain are challenging as the 
overall trend is for the greatest precipitation and the potential 
for heavy or excessive rain focusing to the southeast. Expect one 
batch of showers and storms to be exiting central NC off to the east 
and southeast on Friday morning followed by a bit of a lull across 
much of the area during the day. As another disturbance aloft 
approaches, forcing for ascent should increase, and showers and 
storms will likely redevelop on Friday night. The rain should be 
lighter and less convective across northern areas but in locations 
south of U.S. route 64, instability and deep moisture will buckle 
north and the precipitation will be more widespread, convective and 
potentially heavy. The WPC QPF forecast for Friday and Friday night 
ranges less than 0.25 inches in the Triad and near the VA border, 
0.25 to 0.5 inches in the Triangle and Rocky Mount areas and 0.5 to 
1.0 inches in the Sandhills and southern Coastal Plain. With this in 
mind, will keep the current expiration time on the Flood Watch as is 
while noting that it may be necessary to extend the watch across 
southern and southeastern areas. Friday will be another day with 
below average temperatures, as much as 10 to 15 degrees below 
average in the north with highs ranging from the mid 70s in the 
Triad to the lower 80s in the Sandhills. 


Key Message 3... After another cool and rainy day Saturday, the 
chance of rain will decrease and temperatures will return to normal 
late July values.
